key_results: The Fourier transform is linear for every member of the transform family: scaling a signal scales its transform, and adding signals adds their transforms. Addition must be performed on real and imaginary parts, not directly on polar magnitudes and phases. [Chapter 10, Linearity of the Fourier Transform, Figs. 10-1–10-2]

A shift of s samples in time leaves the magnitude spectrum unchanged and adds the linear phase term 2πsf; equivalently, time position is encoded in phase slope. A signal symmetric about sample zero has zero phase, while left-right symmetry elsewhere produces linear phase. [Chapter 10, Characteristics of the Phase, Fig. 10-3]

Changing the sign of phase—complex conjugation—flips a time signal left-for-right. Therefore convolution uses A(f)B(f), correlation uses A(f)B*(f), and X(f)X*(f) produces a zero-phase spectrum corresponding to a symmetric autocorrelation-like time signal. [Chapter 10, Characteristics of the Phase]

The DFT alone treats both domains as periodic: sample N−1 neighbors sample 0, and a one-period view is only safe when operations do not overflow a period. Excess extent wraps into adjacent periods as time-domain or frequency-domain aliasing. [Chapter 10, Periodic Nature of the DFT, Figs. 10-8–10-10]

Discrete sinusoids admit positive-, negative-, and infinitely many aliased-frequency descriptions that pass through the same samples. The ordinary 0-to-0.5 spectrum is one selected interval of a periodic frequency domain, not the only mathematical description. [Chapter 10, Periodic Nature of the DFT, Fig. 10-11]

Compression in one domain expands the other. For discrete signals this statement is conditioned on aliasing and on an assumed underlying continuous waveform; interpolation and decimation are resampling interpretations of the same relationship. [Chapter 10, Compression and Expansion, Multirate Methods, Fig. 10-12]

Frequency-domain zero padding interpolates a frequency-encoded time sequence without adding frequencies: Smith's 50-to-400-sample recipe pads to a 64-point DFT, extends its 33-bin real and imaginary spectra to 257 bins, and applies a 512-point inverse DFT. Discontinuities ring because the periodic bandlimited interpolant exhibits Gibbs behavior. [Chapter 10, Compression and Expansion, Multirate Methods, Fig. 10-13]

Multiplication in time corresponds to convolution in frequency. In amplitude modulation, multiplication by a carrier shifts the baseband spectrum to the carrier, producing carrier, upper sideband, and lower sideband; the lower sideband makes the otherwise abstract negative-frequency copy operationally visible. [Chapter 10, Multiplying Signals (Amplitude Modulation), Fig. 10-14]

The DTFT is the transform between an aperiodic discrete time signal and a periodic continuous spectrum. It appears as the zero-padded DFT limit as N approaches infinity and is principally an analytic tool because its sums and integrals are infinite. [Chapter 10, The Discrete Time Fourier Transform, Eqs. 10-1–10-2]

Parseval's relation expresses conservation of signal energy between the time and frequency domains; for Smith's real-DFT convention, DC and Nyquist require special √2 endpoint scaling and the spectrum-side energy sum carries a 2/N factor. [Chapter 10, Parseval's Relation, Eq. 10-3]

A time-domain impulse transforms to constant magnitude and linear phase; its sample position sets the number of sinusoidal cycles in the rectangular real/imaginary spectrum. By DFT duality, every time sample contributes one cosine to the real spectrum and one negative sine to the imaginary spectrum. [Chapter 11, Delta Function Pairs, Figs. 11-1–11-2]

A rectangular pulse and a sinc are a transform pair. The exact discrete spectrum includes aliasing through sin(πf) in the denominator; replacing that factor by πf gives the unaliased continuous approximation. The first spectral zero occurs where one complete sinusoidal cycle fits inside the pulse. [Chapter 11, The Sinc Function, Eqs. 11-1–11-2 and Figs. 11-3–11-4]

A rectangular frequency response corresponds to the sinc impulse response of an ideal low-pass filter. A triangle transforms to sinc squared because the triangle is the self-convolution of a rectangle; a Gaussian is its own transform shape with 2πσ_f=1/σ_t; and modulating a Gaussian by a sinusoid shifts its Gaussian spectrum. [Chapter 11, Other Transform Pairs, Eqs. 11-3–11-4 and Fig. 11-5]

At a discontinuity, a partial Fourier reconstruction rings and overshoots by roughly 9%. Adding harmonics narrows the ringing but does not reduce its peak; the continuous limit converges to the step midpoint at the discontinuity and to zero total error energy. [Chapter 11, Gibbs Effect, Fig. 11-6]

A waveform periodic at f contains only harmonics at integer multiples of f. Horizontal antisymmetry eliminates even harmonics, while nonlinear processing of sampled data can create above-Nyquist harmonics that alias back and masquerade as low-level noise. [Chapter 11, Harmonics, Figs. 11-7–11-8]

The chirp system has unit magnitude response and parabolic phase, yielding an impulse response whose instantaneous frequency sweeps with time. The phase-conjugate antichirp reverses it, enabling radar pulse compression: transmitter hardware handles a long energetic chirp while the receiver recovers a narrow timing pulse. [Chapter 11, Chirp Signals, Eq. 11-7 and Figs. 11-9–11-10]

A real N-point time signal can be transformed with a complex FFT by putting it in the real input array and zeroing the imaginary input. The useful real-DFT bins are 0 through N/2; the remaining complex-DFT bins are generated by even symmetry in the real part and odd symmetry in the imaginary part. [Chapter 12, Real DFT Using the Complex DFT, Fig. 12-1 and Table 12-1]

The radix-2 FFT recursively separates even and odd samples through log2 N stages, equivalent to bit-reversal reordering. It then synthesizes one-point spectra with butterfly operations that duplicate spectra, apply phase-shift sinusoids, and add paired results. [Chapter 12, How the FFT Works, Figs. 12-2–12-7]

The presented FFT is an in-place computation: the real and imaginary input arrays are overwritten by intermediate and output data. Variants such as decimation-in-time and decimation-in-frequency move bit reversal but produce the same DFT and comparable performance. [Chapter 12, FFT Programs, Tables 12-3–12-4]

A forward FFT can implement the inverse FFT by negating the imaginary spectrum, applying the forward transform, dividing both time-domain parts by N, and negating the imaginary output again. Round-trip reconstruction and expected even/odd symmetries are the chapter's two essential correctness tests. [Chapter 12, FFT Programs, Table 12-5]

Direct correlation computes the DFT in O(N²), while the FFT takes O(N log2 N). In the book's 100 MHz Pentium benchmark, a 1024-point transform drops from about 25 seconds to about 70 milliseconds—over 300× faster—and fewer operations also reduce roundoff error. [Chapter 12, Speed and Precision Comparisons, Eqs. 12-1–12-2 and Figs. 12-8–12-9]

Real-FFT variants exploit zero imaginary input and conjugate symmetry for about a 30% speed improvement; packing two real sequences into the real and imaginary input parts and separating their spectra with even/odd decomposition saves about 40% when two transforms are needed. [Chapter 12, Further Speed Increases, Figs. 12-10–12-11]

The continuous delta is defined operationally as an infinitesimally brief, unit-area impulse at zero. Real inputs act as impulses only relative to a slower system; their exact shape becomes irrelevant while output amplitude scales with input area. [Chapter 13, The Delta Function, Fig. 13-1]

Continuous convolution is the integral y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. Its input-side interpretation sums shifted, scaled impulse responses; its output-side interpretation integrates the input weighted by a flipped and shifted impulse response. [Chapter 13, Convolution, Eq. 13-1 and Figs. 13-2–13-3]

For an RC low-pass, h(t)=αe^(−αt) for t≥0 and zero before, with α=1/RC. Convolution with a one-second rectangular pulse must be evaluated in no-overlap, partial-overlap, and full-overlap regions, yielding an exponential charge followed by exponential discharge. [Chapter 13, Convolution, Figs. 13-4–13-6]

Continuous convolution problems can be simplified by differentiating piecewise-polynomial inputs into impulses, convolving by inspection, and integrating the result; constants of integration must restore lost DC terms. If only a waveform is required, discretizing and numerically convolving may be more useful than forcing a closed form. [Chapter 13, Convolution, Fig. 13-7]

For continuous aperiodic signals, Fourier synthesis integrates scaled sine and cosine waves over continuous frequency, while analysis correlates the signal with those sinusoids over all time. Transforming the RC impulse response gives its familiar low-pass magnitude and phase. [Chapter 13, The Fourier Transform, Eqs. 13-2–13-3 and Figs. 13-8–13-9]

The Fourier series represents a continuous periodic signal with a DC term plus sine and cosine harmonics of its fundamental. The coefficients are correlations over any one complete period; even signals need only cosine coefficients and odd signals only sine coefficients. [Chapter 13, The Fourier Series, Eqs. 13-4–13-5]

Every linear filter is equivalently specified by impulse, step, or frequency response: running-summing the impulse response gives the step response, and transforming it gives the frequency response. Convolution implementations are FIR; recursive implementations are generally IIR even though both still possess an impulse response. [Chapter 14, Filter Basics, Fig. 14-1]

Decibels express ratios: 10log10(P2/P1) for power and 20log10(A2/A1) for amplitude. Thus −3 dB corresponds to amplitude 0.707 and half power, while each ±20 dB is a factor of ten in amplitude. [Chapter 14, Filter Basics, Eq. 14-1]

Filter design begins by locating the information: time-domain information is carried by when events occur and by waveform amplitude, whereas frequency-domain information is carried by relationships among many samples. These incompatible encodings make step response the primary criterion for the former and frequency response for the latter. [Chapter 14, How Information Is Represented in Signals]

Time-domain filter quality is judged by 10–90% risetime, overshoot, and linear-phase symmetry between rising and falling edges. Frequency-domain quality is judged by transition width/roll-off, passband ripple, and stopband attenuation. These objectives inherently trade against one another. [Chapter 14, Time Domain Parameters and Frequency Domain Parameters, Figs. 14-2–14-4]

Spectral inversion converts a symmetric low-pass FIR kernel h[n] to high-pass by forming δ[n]−h[n]; spectral reversal multiplies alternate kernel samples by −1, shifting the response by half the sampling rate. Adding low- and high-pass kernels forms band-reject, while convolving them forms band-pass. [Chapter 14, High-Pass, Band-Pass and Band-Reject Filters, Figs. 14-5–14-9]

Smith classifies filters by both purpose and implementation: moving-average FIR versus single-pole IIR for time-domain work, windowed-sinc FIR versus Chebyshev IIR for frequency separation, and direct custom FIR versus iterative recursive design for specialized responses. [Chapter 14, Filter Classification, Table 14-1]

An M-point moving average is convolution with a unit-area rectangular kernel; symmetric placement avoids relative delay but requires odd M. The direct implementation performs M additions per output, with output boundaries shortened by the kernel support. [Chapter 15, Implementation by Convolution, Eq. 15-1 and Table 15-1]

For white random noise, an M-point average reduces noise standard deviation by √M. Given a fixed edge width, equal weighting is optimal because no independent noisy sample deserves preference, making the moving average optimal for noise reduction at a specified step sharpness. [Chapter 15, Noise Reduction vs. Step Response, Fig. 15-1]

The moving-average response is sin(πfM)/(M sin πf): excellent for smoothing but poor for frequency separation because roll-off is slow and stopband sidelobes are large. [Chapter 15, Frequency Response, Eq. 15-2 and Fig. 15-2]

Repeated moving averages convolve rectangular kernels into a triangle and then a Gaussian-like shape; each pass multiplies the frequency response. Gaussian and Blackman kernels improve stopband behavior but retain roughly comparable noise-versus-edge performance and require slower direct convolution. [Chapter 15, Relatives of the Moving Average Filter, Figs. 15-3–15-4]

A moving average admits the O(1)-per-sample recursion y[i]=y[i−1]+x[i+p]−x[i−q]. Integer arithmetic avoids accumulated roundoff; a floating-point version should preserve the running sum in double precision to prevent a drifting offset. [Chapter 15, Recursive Implementation, Eq. 15-3 and Table 15-2]

A windowed-sinc low-pass begins with the ideal rectangular response and infinite sinc kernel, truncates and shifts the kernel, then multiplies it by a smooth window to suppress the endpoint discontinuity responsible for Gibbs ripple. [Chapter 16, Strategy of the Windowed-Sinc, Fig. 16-1]

The Hamming window rolls off about 20% faster, but Blackman provides materially better passband/stopband error: roughly 0.02% (−74 dB stopband) versus Hamming's 0.2% (−53 dB). Smith recommends Blackman when a slightly longer kernel is acceptable. [Chapter 16, Strategy of the Windowed-Sinc, Eqs. 16-1–16-2 and Fig. 16-2]

For the book's windowed-sinc design convention, kernel span M is approximately 4/BW, with BW measured across the 99%-to-1% transition and cutoff defined at half amplitude. M is even, the kernel has M+1 samples, and coefficients are normalized so their sum is one. [Chapter 16, Designing the Filter, Eqs. 16-3–16-4]

The symmetric windowed-sinc kernel provides linear phase but an oscillatory, overshooting step response. It is therefore a frequency-separation filter, not a good choice when waveform shape carries the information. [Chapter 16, Designing the Filter, Fig. 16-4]

The worked EEG design separates 7–12 Hz alpha rhythm from 17–20 Hz beta rhythm at 100 samples/s with a 101-point Hamming low-pass near 14 Hz; the audio signaling example uses an 801-point Blackman band-pass to isolate 1960–2040 Hz at a 10 kHz sample rate with 50 Hz transitions. [Chapter 16, Examples of Windowed-Sinc Filters, Figs. 16-5–16-6 and Tables 16-1–16-2]

Cascading identical windowed-sinc filters squares their magnitude response: two −74 dB Blackman stages yield roughly −148 dB stopband attenuation. Extremely long kernels can make transitions arbitrarily sharp, with execution time and numerical precision—not unexpected instability—as the main limits. [Chapter 16, Pushing It to the Limit, Fig. 16-7]

An arbitrary FIR response is designed by specifying magnitude and phase samples, applying an inverse FFT, circularly shifting the aliased impulse response, truncating it, and windowing it. Re-transforming a zero-padded kernel tests the actual continuous response; increasing kernel length improves the match between specified samples. [Chapter 17, Arbitrary Frequency Response, Tables 17-1 and Figs. 17-1–17-2]

Known-system deconvolution divides the desired output spectrum by the unwanted system response using complex division, then designs a practical FIR kernel from that quotient. It becomes unstable where the original system strongly attenuates or nulls frequencies, because inverse gain amplifies modeling error and noise. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution, Figs. 17-4–17-5]

Blind deconvolution has no general solution because the parasitic response is unknown. The Caruso restoration example estimates recording-horn coloration by comparing averaged old-recording and modern-reference spectra, with homomorphic processing used in the cited historical work for a better estimate. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution, Fig. 17-6]

Different filters are optimal under different objective functions: moving average gives the fastest step for a noise reduction, matched filtering maximizes peak detectability in white noise, and Wiener filtering uses H(f)=S²/(S²+N²) to maximize overall output signal-to-noise power. [Chapter 17, Optimal Filters, Eq. 17-1 and Figs. 17-7–17-9]

Overlap-add partitions a long input into zero-padded blocks, convolves each independently, and sums their overlapping output tails. Because an N-sample block convolved with an M-sample kernel produces N+M−1 samples, adequate padding is what makes the segmented result exactly equal to full direct convolution. [Chapter 18, The Overlap-Add Method, Fig. 18-1]

FFT convolution replaces each block's direct convolution with FFT → complex spectral multiplication → inverse FFT. Transform length must be at least the output-block length to prevent circular wraparound; a 128-point block and 129-point kernel therefore use 256-point FFTs. [Chapter 18, FFT Convolution, Fig. 18-2]

The full program example filters 10,000,000 samples with a 400-point kernel using 16,000 blocks of 625 input samples and 1024-point transforms, retaining 399 samples of overlap between blocks and producing 10,000,399 output samples. [Chapter 18, FFT Convolution, Table 18-1]

The implementation crossover is hardware-dependent but lies around 40–80 kernel samples; Smith's rule of thumb is direct convolution below roughly 60 and FFT convolution above it. FFT convolution's operation count grows slowly enough that a 16,000-point kernel costs only about twice a 64-point kernel, and fewer operations also reduce roundoff. [Chapter 18, Speed Improvements, Fig. 18-3]
pedagogy: This shard continues Smith's intuition-first, engineering-practice approach and deliberately postpones complex-variable formalism even while teaching FFT use. Each concept is presented as a reversible relationship between pictures in two domains, then grounded with an equation, a numeric design rule, and often BASIC-like executable pseudocode. The nine-chapter sequence is unusually coherent: Chapter 10 catalogs transform operations; Chapter 11 turns them into memorable transform pairs and edge phenomena; Chapter 12 makes the DFT computationally practical; Chapter 13 transfers the same ideas to continuous calculus; Chapters 14–17 organize filter choice by where information lives and build increasingly specialized FIR filters; Chapter 18 closes the loop by making long FIR kernels practical. Formal proofs are rare. Smith favors physical thought experiments, dimensional/numerical checks, side-by-side plots, and worked programs, and repeatedly warns that labels such as 'optimal' or abstract equations do not replace problem judgment. There are no conventional end-of-chapter exercises in Chapters 10–18; the learning work is carried by derivations, code tracing, design examples, and interpretive figure sequences. Prerequisites are algebra, trigonometry, elementary probability, basic calculus for Chapter 13, and the earlier chapters' convolution and real-DFT notation; complex mathematics is explicitly not assumed. Some benchmarks, television channel examples, audio/video data rates, and programming syntax are historically dated, but the algorithms, tradeoffs, and diagnostic habits remain pedagogically strong.

gems: The phase chapter's central mnemonic is unusually durable: moving a waveform changes the slope of its phase but not its magnitude. The puzzling pulse centered at N/2 can legitimately be assigned three apparently different phase lines because π and 2π ambiguities make them equivalent. [Chapter 10, Characteristics of the Phase, Fig. 10-3]

Amplitude modulation makes negative frequency 'take human form': the negative-frequency copy of a 300 Hz–3 kHz voice spectrum becomes the physically transmitted lower sideband after shifting by the carrier. [Chapter 10, Multiplying Signals (Amplitude Modulation), Fig. 10-14]

The historical TV multiplexing ledger stacks eighty-two 6 MHz channels, from channel 3 at 60–66 MHz through channel 83 at 884–890 MHz, as a concrete example of frequency translation. [Chapter 10, Multiplying Signals (Amplitude Modulation)]

The 50-to-400-sample interpolation recipe is a ready-made lab: one smooth waveform interpolates gracefully, while an edge-rich waveform develops dramatic periodic ringing despite preserving exactly the original frequency content. [Chapter 10, Compression and Expansion, Multirate Methods, Fig. 10-13]

The sinc's zero crossings become intuitive through correlation: a rectangular pulse accumulates a sinusoid to zero whenever an integer number of cycles fits exactly inside its width. [Chapter 11, The Sinc Function]

Gibbs ringing supplies a striking limit experiment: more harmonics keep the overshoot near 9% while squeezing it to zero width, resolving the old objection that sinusoids cannot reconstruct a corner. [Chapter 11, Gibbs Effect, Fig. 11-6]
A nominal 1 kHz TTL square wave with nanosecond edges can carry harmonics nearly to 100 MHz—the ten-thousandth harmonic—making 'sharp edges require high frequencies' concrete. [Chapter 11, Harmonics]

Radar chirp compression resolves the conflict between range resolution and transmitter power: stretch energy into a long sweep for transmission, then use an antichirp to recover a narrow timing pulse. [Chapter 11, Chirp Signals]

The FFT is introduced with two memorable comparisons: its speedup is like flying rather than walking, and its foundational status in DSP is likened to the transistor in electronics. [Chapter 12, introduction and Further Speed Increases]

The 1024-point benchmark turns complexity into an unforgettable gap: about 25 seconds by direct correlation versus about 70 milliseconds by FFT on the reference machine. [Chapter 12, Speed and Precision Comparisons]

Mars and Sirius appear similarly point-like to the unaided eye even though their geometry differs enormously because both are impulses to the visual system; a telescope resolves Mars as a disk while Sirius remains a point-spread response. [Chapter 13, The Delta Function]

The chapter stretches 'impulse' across scales: a picosecond pulse can be impulsive to microwave electronics, while a years-long volcanic eruption can be impulsive relative to millennial geology. [Chapter 13, The Delta Function]

A one-resistor, one-capacitor circuit carries the whole continuous-systems story: its exponential impulse response is convolved region-by-region with a square pulse to derive charging and discharging without hiding the limits of integration. [Chapter 13, Convolution, Figs. 13-4–13-6]

A 1 kHz, 1 V pulse train at duty cycle 0.2 still reconstructs poorly with fourteen harmonics, making slow Fourier-series convergence and Gibbs overshoot visible in a concrete coefficient table. [Chapter 13, The Fourier Series, Figs. 13-11–13-12]

Crystal oscillators top out near 10 MHz in the chapter's account, so a 150 MHz source is built by distorting a lower-frequency stable oscillator and isolating a selected harmonic with band-pass stages. [Chapter 13, The Fourier Series]

The fetal-EKG example makes filter purpose explicit: a desired baby's heartbeat is mixed with the mother's breathing and heartbeat, so filtering is signal separation rather than merely smoothing. [Chapter 14, Filter Basics]

Smith's two-signal thought experiment—single solar-light samples carry event information, while no single wine-glass audio sample reveals its resonant frequency—cleanly separates time-encoded from frequency-encoded information. [Chapter 14, How Information Is Represented in Signals]

The moving average is defended against engineering embarrassment: its simplicity is not a compromise but the exact optimal equal-weight solution for white-noise reduction at fixed edge width. [Chapter 15, Noise Reduction vs. Step Response]

A 100-point moving average reduces random noise tenfold, yet recursive evaluation still needs only one addition and one subtraction per output after initialization. [Chapter 15, Noise Reduction vs. Step Response and Recursive Implementation]

A fiber-optic pulse naturally exits Gaussian-shaped because photons take different paths, tying repeated-convolution/Gaussian theory to a physical propagation effect. [Chapter 15, Relatives of the Moving Average Filter]

The EEG design turns abstract passbands into physiology: eyes-closed alpha activity occupies about 7–12 Hz, eyes-open beta about 17–20 Hz, and a 101-point filter at 100 samples/s separates them. [Chapter 16, Examples of Windowed-Sinc Filters]

The extreme windowed-sinc example asks for a 1 mV signal riding on a 120 V power line, motivating at least −120 dB attenuation and then obtaining about −148 dB by filtering twice. [Chapter 16, Pushing It to the Limit]

A 32,001-point FIR is specified to pass DC–1000 Hz within 0.02% and reject everything above 1001 Hz to below 0.02%, dramatizing how long kernels buy narrow transitions. [Chapter 16, Pushing It to the Limit, Fig. 16-7]

Gamma-ray pulse pile-up makes deconvolution tangible: sodium-iodide scintillation decays over hundreds of nanoseconds, overlapping events corrupt energy estimates, and inverse filtering narrows the pulses until noise/model error sets the limit. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution, Figs. 17-3–17-5]

The deconvolution chapter's blunt information limit is pedagogically useful: once an attenuated frequency falls below noise—or is reduced to zero—no processing can recover it; inverse gain only amplifies ignorance. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution]

Restoring Enrico Caruso recordings becomes a historical blind-deconvolution case: unknown horn resonances are estimated by comparing averaged spectra of old recordings with modern performances and then counter-equalized. [Chapter 17, Deconvolution, Fig. 17-6]

The three 'optimal' filters produce visually unimpressive differences, which Smith uses to teach a broader lesson: optimizing one metric does not automatically optimize the human task or justify added complexity. [Chapter 17, Optimal Filters, Fig. 17-9]

The 10-million-sample FFT-convolution example is a complete bookkeeping set piece: 16,000 blocks ×625 samples, a 400-point kernel, 1024-point FFTs, 399 saved overlap samples, and exactly 10,000,399 outputs. [Chapter 18, FFT Convolution, Table 18-1]

For long kernels, cost becomes surprisingly flat: a 16,000-point FFT-convolution kernel takes only about twice the execution time of a 64-point one in the chapter's rule-of-thumb comparison. [Chapter 18, Speed Improvements]
